title: They Evacuated the World's Remotest Island. Then Went Back.
question: Why do people live on Tristan da Cunha?
message: This video tells curious adults that people first stayed on one of the most remote inhabited islands on Earth because a British garrison, sent there because of Napoleon, left behind a corporal who chose to stay, and that after a volcano forced everyone out in 1961, the islanders voted to go home to their shared land, their lobster and their own way of running things.
angle: People live on Tristan da Cunha because a British garrison posted there to guard against a rescue of Napoleon left behind a corporal who stayed and a community built on shared land, and because after the nineteen sixty-one eruption the islanders voted to return to land they own together, a lobster fishery and an island they run themselves, despite no airstrip, a voyage of about six days from Cape Town, a harbour that is safe only on calm days and serious medical care a sea voyage away.

Không tóm ba vế, không 'Would I move there?', không cặp 'It suits / It does not suit', không 'I changed my mind', không chương theo mốc giờ. scenes.narration: The island is Tristan da Cunha, in the middle of the South Atlantic. Guinness lists it as the most remote inhabited island, measured by the distance to the nearest other people. As of November twenty twenty-six, it counted about two hundred and twenty islanders. In England they'd had buses, shops and dry socks. Nearly all of them still voted for the island with the volcano. I wanted to know why. But first, an older question. Who would start a village out there at all? I guessed wrong. Twice. The answer, it turned out, lived on a different island.

scenes.narration: There is no airstrip on Tristan. You go by sea, from Cape Town in South Africa, about two thousand eight hundred kilometres away. That's roughly seventeen hundred and fifty miles. The crossing usually takes around six days. Only nine sailings from Cape Town were on the twenty twenty-six schedule. I took the small backpack this time. I got a bunk on a fishing ship and drew our route in my notebook, one dot for every hour. By the third day, the dots had gone off the edge of the page and across the table. The sea stayed grey. On Monday it was grey. By Thursday it was grey with real commitment. I packed and unpacked the small backpack until it filed a complaint. Then, one morning, a cloud sat on the horizon and refused to move. There was a mountain under it.

scenes.narration: Then came the part the ticket doesn't cover. Getting off. Big ships can't tie up at Tristan, so ours anchored offshore, and people and cargo went in by small boat. I stepped down into it just as it rose up to meet me. We met halfway. Not gracefully. Up close, the island is basically one volcano, just over two thousand metres tall, about sixty-seven hundred feet, wearing a cloud like a hat. The only village sits on a strip of flat green land at its foot. Officially, it's Edinburgh of the Seven Seas, named after a visit from Queen Victoria's son Alfred, the Duke of Edinburgh, in eighteen sixty-seven. The islanders don't call it that. It's the Settlement. I stood on the shore with my small backpack and thought, nobody picks this on purpose.

He sailed on. The first landing anyone recorded came in sixteen forty-three, by a Dutch ship. Second theory. A shipwreck. Somebody's terrible day at sea, a raft, a beach, a brave new life. I walked the shore with a stick, looking for the wreck that started it all. I found a potato. Shipwrecks do turn up in this story, later. They didn't start it. The real beginning came from much further north.

scenes.narration: Napoleon. After his final defeat, Britain exiled Napoleon to St Helena, another lonely island, about two thousand four hundred kilometres north of Tristan. Britain worried the French could use Tristan as a base for a rescue. It also wanted to stop American ships using it as a base, as they had in the War of eighteen twelve. So on the fourteenth of August, eighteen sixteen, British troops landed and claimed the island. A garrison, guarding an emperor who wasn't there, on an island almost nobody could reach. I pictured it as locking the back door of a house across town, just in case a burglar uses it as a shortcut. About a year later, the navy decided the island wasn't worth the bother. The soldiers sailed away in November eighteen seventeen. Soldiers leave. That's their job. So why is there still a village?

scenes.narration: Because one of them asked to stay. Corporal William Glass, a Scotsman, stayed on with his wife and children. Then he and two stonemasons signed an agreement to share everything equally, the animals, the stores and the profits. Nobody in the group would stand above the others. Others kept arriving. A sailor from Hastings. A Dutchman whose ship was wrecked. An American whaler, and later an American whaling captain. In eighteen twenty-seven, a ship's captain brought five women over from St Helena. In eighteen ninety-two, two Italian sailors came ashore from a wrecked ship, the Italia, and stayed. Today the island has seven family names. It works a bit like a guestbook where every signature turned into a family. I signed it too. In pencil. Just in case.

scenes.narration: Next morning, I auditioned for island life. First job, the Potato Patches. They're stone-walled fields a few kilometres west of the village, and every family farms there, at least part time. All the land on Tristan is owned in common. No outsider can buy a piece of it. Picture a garden the whole street plants together, where you look after your own rows but can never put them up for sale. The potatoes go into the same walled plots, year after year. I was handed a fork. I dug very carefully. I lifted out one potato and held it up like a trophy. A cow on the other side of the wall looked at it. Then it went back to eating. Spare potatoes end up as cattle feed. The cow had seen better trophies.

scenes.narration: Second job, lobster. Tristan rock lobster is what the island lives on. There are even two lobsters on the coat of arms. The fishery brings in roughly four-fifths of the territory's revenue, according to the Marine Stewardship Council. But the boats only go out when the sea allows, and estimates of how many days that adds up to vary a lot. So the alarm clock here isn't a clock. At five in the morning, if two veteran fishermen like the look of the sky, someone takes a hammer to an old oxygen bottle. That's the fishing gong. I slept through it. I slept through it again. On the next calm morning, I slept sitting up in my boots, right next to the bottle. Each little boat carries two fishermen, who haul up their traps with a winch. I mostly held a rope and tried not to become cargo.

scenes.narration: Third job. I asked for a cow. According to the island government, at least as of a few years ago, each household could keep one breeding cow. Sheep were limited too, so the grass doesn't get eaten bare. Think of a shared kitchen where everyone gets the same ladle, so nobody empties the pot. I don't have a household on Tristan. So, no cow. I patted somebody else's cow instead. It allowed this, briefly. Walking back along the walls, I noticed that every rule I'd bumped into had the same shape. The shared land. The gong. The one cow. Each one, as far as I could tell, keeps the island from being used up. On the beach, I'd decided nobody picks this on purpose. Next to that cow, I wanted to pick it myself.

scenes.narration: The day before my ship left, I went to the post office to send this postcard. Start with the stamp. Tristan had no stamps of its own until nineteen fifty-two. Before that, letters waited for a passing ship. In nineteen forty-six, a man named Allan Crawford drew a set of stamp designs and sent them to London with a petition. Every design had a penguin on it. The price was in potatoes. One penny, or four potatoes. London said no. In twenty fifteen, the island finally printed those designs as real stamps. That's the one on my postcard. Now zoom out, from the stamp to the post office. When the island's stamps finally arrived, collectors around the world wanted them, and they paid off from the very first year. Zoom out again, to the whole economy. Stamps and coins sold to collectors still bring foreign money in today. I paid in coins. I did ask about potatoes. One last zoom. My postcard left in a mail bag, on a ship, via Cape Town, taking the long way home.

scenes.narration: That afternoon, I walked to the eastern edge of the village, where the ground suddenly turns dark and rough. From August nineteen sixty-one, the island kept shaking. On the eighth of October, a big tremor brought rock down east of the village. That night, everyone slept in the huts out at the Potato Patches. Then a crack opened between the houses and the fish cannery, and the ground swelled. By the tenth, it was a new volcano. Two fishing ships, the Tristania and the Frances Repetto, carried everyone to Nightingale Island for the night. The next day, a passing Dutch liner picked them up. Two hundred and sixty-four islanders went to Cape Town, and on to England. They took what they could carry. The lava destroyed the cannery. Most of the houses survived, with nobody in them.

scenes.narration: Back home, I put the postcard face down for this part. In England, the islanders ended up at an old air force camp at Calshot, near Southampton, from January nineteen sixty-two. They found work quickly. By the end of February, a hundred and thirteen of them had jobs. But they had little resistance to the flu going around, and the winter that followed was bitter. In July nineteen sixty-two, the British government told Parliament the islanders should stay in England. scenes.narration: In December nineteen sixty-two, the adults held a secret ballot. A hundred and forty-eight voted to go back. Five voted to stay. Picture being handed the keys to a big city, with buses, shops and a doctor down the road. Now picture handing them back, and asking for the key to a small house beside a volcano that erupted the year before. I tried that vote on myself, about my own street. I like my street. I raised one hand. The other one stayed in my pocket. In April nineteen sixty-three, fifty-one islanders landed home first. On the tenth of November, the main group of a hundred and ninety-eight arrived. My best guess at why? England had more of almost everything. It didn't have their land, shared between them, or their say in how it was run.

scenes.narration: The next morning, I waited at the harbour for the small boat out to my ship. It opened in nineteen sixty-seven, a few years after the islanders came home. They named it Calshot, after the village in England that took them in. The entrance is about eleven metres wide, roughly thirty-six feet. And the weather allows boats in and out safely on only about seventy days a year. Think of a shop that opens about one day in five, and never says which. While I waited, I added up the rest. The hospital usually has two doctors, and serious cases go to Cape Town by sea. So do mothers, to give birth. In twenty oh eight, the fish factory burned down and took the island's power station with it. Full power took about a month to come back. My plan to move here was losing pages. Then the boat came, and I almost didn't get in.

scenes.narration: So, the postcard. I wrote it on deck, with the island shrinking behind the ship, and I haven't read it since. It says: Dear me. You can't move here. Outsiders can't buy land, and you can't settle without family on the island. You asked anyway. The harbour opens when the sea agrees. The big hospital is about a week away. Groceries get ordered months ahead. Good for anyone patient who likes their neighbours. Bad for anyone in a hurry. You slept through the gong. Twice. You still want to live here. Love, me. Reading it at my desk, I agree with every word, including the part where they wouldn't have me. It's their island, by family and by ballot. I'm stamping it anyway. WOULD MOVE. If they ever need someone to hold a rope and not become cargo, I'm packed. What would you sail a week to get back to?

verdict.label: WOULD MOVE
verdict.reason: Shared land, a lobster fishery and an island run by its own people won Wob over, and the costs are real (a harbour that opens on calm days, serious care a voyage away, orders placed months ahead); but newcomers can't buy land or settle without family on the island, so the move stays a wish, and Wob still sleeps through the gong.

claims.quote: I posted it from an island that everyone once had to leave. A volcano. They were taken to England, then voted to go back.
claims.statement: In October 1961 a volcanic eruption next to the Settlement forced the entire population of Tristan da Cunha to evacuate; the islanders were taken via Cape Town to England, and in a secret ballot in December 1962 they voted to return.

claims.quote: Guinness lists it as the most remote inhabited island, measured by the distance to the nearest other people.
claims.statement: Guinness World Records lists Tristan da Cunha as the most remote inhabited island, measured by its distance (about 2,435 km) to the nearest inhabited land, St Helena.

claims.quote: As of November twenty twenty-six, it counted about two hundred and twenty islanders.
claims.statement: According to the Tristan da Cunha Government's population update of 18 November 2026, there were 220 islanders (18 of them temporarily overseas), plus 40 non-islanders, giving 242 people on the island.

claims.quote: Nearly all of them still voted for the island with the volcano.
claims.statement: In the secret ballot held in December 1962 among adult Tristan islanders living in England, 148 voted to return to Tristan da Cunha and 5 voted against.

claims.quote: There is no airstrip on Tristan.
claims.statement: Tristan da Cunha has no airstrip or airport; the island can only be reached by sea.

claims.quote: You go by sea, from Cape Town in South Africa, about two thousand eight hundred kilometres away. That's roughly seventeen hundred and fifty miles.
claims.statement: Ships to Tristan da Cunha usually sail from Cape Town, South Africa, which is about 2,810 km (1,750 miles) from the island.

claims.quote: The crossing usually takes around six days.
claims.statement: The sea voyage from Cape Town to Tristan da Cunha usually takes about six days (five to eight days depending on the ship, per the 2026 schedule).

claims.quote: Only nine sailings from Cape Town were on the twenty twenty-six schedule.
claims.statement: The Tristan da Cunha Government's 2026 shipping schedule lists nine sailings from Cape Town to Tristan (three by MFV Edinburgh, five by MV Lance and one by SA Agulhas II).

claims.quote: Big ships can't tie up at Tristan, so ours anchored offshore, and people and cargo went in by small boat.
claims.statement: Large ships cannot berth at Tristan da Cunha's small harbour; they anchor offshore and passengers and cargo are transferred ashore by small boat.

claims.quote: Up close, the island is basically one volcano, just over two thousand metres tall, about sixty-seven hundred feet, wearing a cloud like a hat.
claims.statement: Tristan da Cunha is a single volcanic island; its summit, Queen Mary's Peak, rises to just over 2,000 m (about 2,060 m, roughly 6,760 ft) and is often capped by cloud.

claims.quote: The only village sits on a strip of flat green land at its foot.
claims.statement: Tristan da Cunha's only settlement lies on a narrow coastal plain at the foot of the volcano, on the island's north-west side.

claims.quote: Officially, it's Edinburgh of the Seven Seas, named after a visit from Queen Victoria's son Alfred, the Duke of Edinburgh, in eighteen sixty-seven.
claims.statement: The settlement's official name, Edinburgh of the Seven Seas, comes from the 1867 visit of Prince Alfred, Duke of Edinburgh (Queen Victoria's second son), aboard HMS Galatea.

claims.quote: The islanders don't call it that. It's the Settlement.
claims.statement: Tristan islanders do not normally use the name Edinburgh of the Seven Seas; they call the village 'the Settlement'.

claims.quote: A Portuguese commander sighted the island in fifteen oh six, and it still carries his name.
claims.statement: Tristan da Cunha was sighted in 1506 by the Portuguese commander Tristão da Cunha on a voyage towards the Cape of Good Hope, and the island is named after him.

claims.quote: He sailed on. The first landing anyone recorded came in sixteen forty-three, by a Dutch ship.
claims.statement: Tristão da Cunha did not settle the island; the first recorded landing on Tristan da Cunha was made by the crew of the Dutch ship Heemstede in 1643.

claims.quote: Shipwrecks do turn up in this story, later.
claims.statement: Shipwrecks later brought settlers to Tristan da Cunha, for example Pieter Groen from the wrecked Emily in 1836 and two Italian sailors from the Italia in 1892, decades after the island was first settled in 1816–1817.

claims.quote: After his final defeat, Britain exiled Napoleon to St Helena, another lonely island, about two thousand four hundred kilometres north of Tristan.
claims.statement: After his final defeat, Napoleon was held in exile by Britain on St Helena, which is the nearest inhabited place to Tristan da Cunha, about 2,437 km away.

claims.quote: Britain worried the French could use Tristan as a base for a rescue. It also wanted to stop American ships using it as a base, as they had in the War of eighteen twelve.
claims.statement: Britain took Tristan da Cunha in 1816 because it feared France could use the island as a base for an attempt to rescue Napoleon from St Helena, and to stop American ships using it as a base as they had during the War of 1812.

claims.quote: So on the fourteenth of August, eighteen sixteen, British troops landed and claimed the island.
claims.statement: On 14 August 1816 a British garrison landed from HMS Falmouth and formally took possession of Tristan da Cunha.

claims.quote: About a year later, the navy decided the island wasn't worth the bother. The soldiers sailed away in November eighteen seventeen.
claims.statement: The British garrison was withdrawn from Tristan da Cunha in November 1817, aboard HMS Euridice, because the Admiralty judged the island of little strategic value.

claims.quote: Corporal William Glass, a Scotsman, stayed on with his wife and children.
claims.statement: When the garrison left Tristan da Cunha in 1817, Corporal William Glass, a Scot, was given permission to remain on the island with his wife and children.

claims.quote: Then he and two stonemasons signed an agreement to share everything equally, the animals, the stores and the profits. Nobody in the group would stand above the others.
claims.statement: On 7 November 1817 William Glass and two stonemasons signed an agreement to live as a community, sharing stock, stores and profits equally, with no member claiming superiority over the others.

claims.quote: A sailor from Hastings. A Dutchman whose ship was wrecked. An American whaler, and later an American whaling captain.
claims.statement: Later settlers on Tristan da Cunha included Thomas Swain, a sailor from Hastings (1826); Pieter Groen from Katwijk in the Netherlands, shipwrecked on the Emily (1836); Thomas Rogers, an American whaler (1836); and Andrew Hagan, an American whaling captain (1849).

claims.quote: In eighteen twenty-seven, a ship's captain brought five women over from St Helena.
claims.statement: In 1827 Captain Simon Amm of the Duke of Gloucester brought five women from St Helena to Tristan da Cunha.

claims.quote: In eighteen ninety-two, two Italian sailors came ashore from a wrecked ship, the Italia, and stayed.
claims.statement: In 1892 two Italian sailors from Camogli, Andrea Repetto and Gaetano Lavarello, came ashore after their ship, the Italia, caught fire and ran aground at Tristan da Cunha, and they settled on the island.

claims.quote: Today the island has seven family names.
claims.statement: Tristan da Cunha's islanders today share seven surnames: Glass, Swain, Green, Rogers, Hagan, Repetto and Lavarello.

claims.quote: They're stone-walled fields a few kilometres west of the village, and every family farms there, at least part time.
claims.statement: The Potato Patches on Tristan da Cunha are stone-walled fields a few kilometres west of the Settlement, where every island family farms at least part time.

claims.quote: All the land on Tristan is owned in common. No outsider can buy a piece of it.
claims.statement: All land on Tristan da Cunha is held in common, and outsiders are not permitted to buy land on the island.

claims.quote: The potatoes go into the same walled plots, year after year.
claims.statement: Potatoes on Tristan da Cunha are grown in the same walled plots at the Potato Patches year after year, without crop rotation.

claims.quote: Spare potatoes end up as cattle feed.
claims.statement: On Tristan da Cunha, surplus potatoes are fed to cattle.

claims.quote: Tristan rock lobster is what the island lives on. There are even two lobsters on the coat of arms.
claims.statement: The Tristan rock lobster fishery is the foundation of Tristan da Cunha's economy, and the island's coat of arms (granted in 2002) is supported by two Tristan rock lobsters.

claims.quote: The fishery brings in roughly four-fifths of the territory's revenue, according to the Marine Stewardship Council.
claims.statement: According to the Marine Stewardship Council (2020), the Tristan rock lobster fishery provides about 80% of the territory's revenue; the Tristan Government describes lobster royalties as its main source of foreign income without giving a percentage.

claims.quote: But the boats only go out when the sea allows, and estimates of how many days that adds up to vary a lot.
claims.statement: Tristan da Cunha's small lobster boats can only fish on days when weather and sea allow; sources give different figures, from about 30–40 days a year (MSC, 2020) to 18–72 days a season (BBC, 2025).

claims.quote: At five in the morning, if two veteran fishermen like the look of the sky, someone takes a hammer to an old oxygen bottle. That's the fishing gong.
claims.statement: On Tristan da Cunha, fishing days are announced at about 5 a.m. by striking an old oxygen bottle with a hammer (the 'fishing gong'), after two experienced fishermen have judged the weather suitable.

claims.quote: Each little boat carries two fishermen, who haul up their traps with a winch.
claims.statement: Tristan da Cunha's lobster fishery uses small motorboats crewed by two fishermen each, who haul their traps using a winch.

claims.quote: According to the island government, at least as of a few years ago, each household could keep one breeding cow. Sheep were limited too, so the grass doesn't get eaten bare.
claims.statement: According to the Tristan da Cunha Government's farming page (last revised 2019), the Island Council limited each household to one adult breeding cow and also capped sheep numbers to prevent overgrazing; limits may have changed since.

claims.quote: Tristan had no stamps of its own until nineteen fifty-two. Before that, letters waited for a passing ship.
claims.statement: Tristan da Cunha had no postage stamps until 1 January 1952, when St Helena stamps overprinted 'TRISTAN DA CUNHA' were issued; before that, mail was carried by passing ships.

claims.quote: In nineteen forty-six, a man named Allan Crawford drew a set of stamp designs and sent them to London with a petition.
claims.statement: In 1946 Allan Crawford drew a set of nine stamp designs for Tristan da Cunha and sent them with a petition for postage stamps to the British Postmaster General.

claims.quote: Every design had a penguin on it. The price was in potatoes. One penny, or four potatoes. London said no.
claims.statement: Allan Crawford's 1946 Tristan da Cunha 'potato' stamp designs each showed a penguin and were denominated in potatoes (one penny equal to four potatoes); the petition was refused.

claims.quote: In twenty fifteen, the island finally printed those designs as real stamps.
claims.statement: Tristan da Cunha issued Allan Crawford's 1946 'Potato Essays' designs as a set of postage stamps on 8 April 2015.

claims.quote: When the island's stamps finally arrived, collectors around the world wanted them, and they paid off from the very first year.
claims.statement: When Tristan da Cunha's first stamps were issued in 1952, there was worldwide demand from collectors and the stamps produced revenue for the administration from the first year.

claims.quote: Stamps and coins sold to collectors still bring foreign money in today.
claims.statement: Sales of Tristan da Cunha stamps and coins to collectors are a source of foreign income for the island's government today.

claims.quote: My postcard left in a mail bag, on a ship, via Cape Town
claims.statement: Mail to and from Tristan da Cunha is routed via Cape Town and carried by the ships that sail between Cape Town and the island.

claims.quote: That afternoon, I walked to the eastern edge of the village, where the ground suddenly turns dark and rough.
claims.statement: The 1961 eruption on Tristan da Cunha formed a new volcanic cone and lava flow immediately east of the Settlement, only a few hundred feet from the village.

claims.quote: From August nineteen sixty-one, the island kept shaking.
claims.statement: Earth tremors were felt on Tristan da Cunha from August 1961, in the weeks before the October 1961 eruption.

claims.quote: On the eighth of October, a big tremor brought rock down east of the village. That night, everyone slept in the huts out at the Potato Patches.
claims.statement: On 8 October 1961 a strong earthquake caused a rockfall and landslide east of the Settlement, and that night the islanders and expatriates slept in the huts at the Potato Patches.

claims.quote: Then a crack opened between the houses and the fish cannery, and the ground swelled. By the tenth, it was a new volcano.
claims.statement: On 9 October 1961 a fissure opened between the Settlement and the fish cannery and the ground bulged; on 10 October it developed into a new volcanic cone and the island was evacuated.

claims.quote: Two fishing ships, the Tristania and the Frances Repetto, carried everyone to Nightingale Island for the night.
claims.statement: On 10 October 1961 the fishing vessels Tristania and Frances Repetto took the evacuated population of Tristan da Cunha to Nightingale Island, where they spent the night.

claims.quote: The next day, a passing Dutch liner picked them up.
claims.statement: On 11 October 1961 the Dutch liner Tjisadane picked up the evacuated Tristan islanders and took them to Cape Town.

claims.quote: Two hundred and sixty-four islanders went to Cape Town, and on to England.
claims.statement: 264 Tristan islanders were evacuated in 1961, taken to Cape Town and then on to England (arriving at Southampton on 3 November 1961).

claims.quote: The lava destroyed the cannery. Most of the houses survived, with nobody in them.
claims.statement: The 1961 lava flow destroyed Tristan da Cunha's fish cannery, but most of the Settlement's houses were left undamaged.

claims.quote: In England, the islanders ended up at an old air force camp at Calshot, near Southampton, from January nineteen sixty-two.
claims.statement: From January 1962 the evacuated Tristan islanders were housed at a former Royal Air Force camp at Calshot, near Southampton, Hampshire, after first staying at Pendell Camp in Surrey.

claims.quote: By the end of February, a hundred and thirteen of them had jobs.
claims.statement: According to a written answer in the UK House of Commons on 28 February 1962, 113 Tristan islanders in England had found employment and 14 were still seeking work.

claims.quote: But they had little resistance to the flu going around, and the winter that followed was bitter.
claims.statement: In England the Tristan islanders had little immunity to influenza, and they also endured the harsh winter of 1962–63.

claims.quote: In July nineteen sixty-two, the British government told Parliament the islanders should stay in England.
claims.statement: On 24 July 1962 the UK Colonial Secretary told Parliament that the Tristan islanders should remain in Britain, citing the risk of further eruptions and the difficulty of maintaining services and landing on the island.

claims.quote: Meanwhile, a team of scientists visited the volcano and reported that most of the village was still there.
claims.statement: A Royal Society expedition to Tristan da Cunha from January to March 1962 found the eruption less destructive than feared, with most of the Settlement intact.

claims.quote: By September, twelve islanders were back on Tristan to see it for themselves.
claims.statement: A survey party of twelve Tristan islanders left England in August 1962 and reached Tristan da Cunha in early September 1962 to inspect the island.

claims.quote: In December nineteen sixty-two, the adults held a secret ballot. A hundred and forty-eight voted to go back. Five voted to stay.
claims.statement: In a secret ballot organised by the Colonial Office in December 1962, adult Tristan islanders in England voted 148 to 5 in favour of returning to Tristan da Cunha.

claims.quote: In April nineteen sixty-three, fifty-one islanders landed home first.
claims.statement: An advance party of 51 Tristan islanders, who left Tilbury in March 1963, arrived back on Tristan da Cunha on 9 April 1963.

claims.quote: On the tenth of November, the main group of a hundred and ninety-eight arrived.
claims.statement: The main group of 198 Tristan islanders, who sailed from Southampton on the Bornholm on 24 October 1963, arrived back on Tristan da Cunha on 10 November 1963.

claims.quote: It opened in nineteen sixty-seven, a few years after the islanders came home. They named it Calshot, after the village in England that took them in.
claims.statement: Tristan da Cunha's Calshot Harbour opened in 1967 and is named after Calshot in Hampshire, England, where the evacuated islanders were housed in 1962–63.

claims.quote: The entrance is about eleven metres wide, roughly thirty-six feet. And the weather allows boats in and out safely on only about seventy days a year. Think of a shop that opens about one day in five, and never says which.
claims.statement: Calshot Harbour on Tristan da Cunha has an entrance about 11 m (36 ft) wide, and weather conditions make it safe for boats to enter and leave on only about 70 days a year (roughly one day in five).

claims.quote: The hospital usually has two doctors, and serious cases go to Cape Town by sea. So do mothers, to give birth.
claims.statement: Tristan da Cunha's Camogli Healthcare Centre is normally staffed by two doctors; complex and serious cases are transferred to Cape Town, and expectant mothers travel to Cape Town to give birth.

claims.quote: In twenty oh eight, the fish factory burned down and took the island's power station with it. Full power took about a month to come back.
claims.statement: On the night of 12–13 February 2008 Tristan da Cunha's fish factory burned down together with the island's electricity generators; full 24-hour power was restored on 14 March 2008, about a month later.

claims.quote: Outsiders can't buy land, and you can't settle without family on the island.
claims.statement: Outsiders cannot buy land on Tristan da Cunha, and people without a family connection to the island are not normally allowed to settle there.

claims.quote: The big hospital is about a week away.
claims.statement: Serious medical cases from Tristan da Cunha are taken to hospital in Cape Town, a sea voyage of about six days.

claims.quote: Groceries get ordered months ahead.
claims.statement: Goods for Tristan da Cunha's only shop, the Island Store, must be ordered many months before the ship that will bring them.
